title: Where civilisation began
summary: From the first farmers and temples to the first cities and writing, 9500–1250 BCE.

steps.title: Temples before towns
steps.text: Around 9500 BCE, hunter-gatherers in what is now Turkey carved huge stone pillars at Göbekli Tepe. A monument may have come before farming.

steps.title: The first farmers
steps.text: In the Fertile Crescent, people began planting wheat and barley and herding sheep and goats. Food surpluses let villages grow, Jericho among them.

steps.title: Farming spreads
steps.text: Farming spread from village to village. Çatalhöyük in Anatolia held thousands of people in houses entered through the roof. Rice was being domesticated in China around the same time.

steps.title: Temples on the river plain
steps.text: Ubaid villages on the Mesopotamian plain dug irrigation canals and built the first temples at Eridu.

steps.title: The first cities
steps.text: Uruk grew into one of the first true cities, with thousands of people, temples and full-time officials and craftsmen.

steps.title: Writing is invented
steps.text: Sumerian scribes pressed signs into clay to record goods and debts. This was cuneiform, one of the world’s first writing systems.

steps.title: Egypt unites
steps.text: Along the Nile, Upper and Lower Egypt were united under one king, starting 3,000 years of pharaohs.

steps.title: Pyramids in Peru
steps.text: In the Americas, Caral–Supe built platform mounds in the Peruvian desert, independently of the Old World.

steps.title: Cities of the Indus
steps.text: In South Asia, planned cities like Mohenjo-daro had grid streets and covered drains. Their script is still undeciphered.

steps.title: China’s first writing
steps.text: Shang kings carved questions to their ancestors on bones. These oracle bones are the oldest Chinese writing and the ancestor of today’s characters.

title: The Silk Road
summary: How a web of trade routes linked China and the Mediterranean, 130 BCE–1450.

steps.title: An envoy goes west
steps.text: Han China sent the envoy Zhang Qian into Central Asia. His reports opened regular trade westward.

steps.title: The middlemen
steps.text: Goods passed from hand to hand. The Kushans and Parthians in the middle grew rich, and Rome paid in gold for Chinese silk.

steps.title: Ideas travel too
steps.text: Buddhism spread from India through Kushan lands into China along the same routes.

steps.title: Tang Chang’an
steps.text: Under the Tang, Chang’an was one of the largest cities in the world, full of Sogdian, Persian and Arab merchants.

steps.title: Paper reaches the west
steps.text: Papermaking spread from China to Baghdad, where the Abbasid House of Wisdom translated and copied books.

steps.title: The Mongol peace
steps.text: The Mongol Empire made the whole route safer. Marco Polo travelled to Kublai Khan’s court.

steps.title: Plague on the road
steps.text: The Black Death travelled the same routes and killed a huge share of Eurasia’s people.

steps.title: The sea takes over
steps.text: As empires broke up and ships improved, more trade moved to sea routes across the Indian Ocean.

title: Rise and fall of Rome
summary: From a small city to a Mediterranean empire, and what came after, 753 BCE–1453.

steps.title: A city on seven hills
steps.text: By legend Rome was founded in 753 BCE. For centuries it was a small city among many in Italy.

steps.title: The Republic
steps.text: Romans expelled their king and ruled through elected magistrates and the Senate.

steps.title: Rome against Carthage
steps.text: In the Punic Wars Rome fought Carthage for the western Mediterranean. Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants, but Rome won.

steps.title: Civil wars
steps.text: Conquests made generals rich and powerful. Julius Caesar seized power and was murdered in 44 BCE.

steps.title: The first emperor
steps.text: Augustus ended the civil wars and became the first emperor, beginning two centuries of relative peace.

steps.title: The greatest extent
steps.text: Under Trajan the empire reached its largest size, about 5 million km².

steps.title: Plague and crisis
steps.text: The Antonine Plague and later the crisis of the 3rd century brought war, inflation and frequent changes of emperor.

steps.title: A new capital
steps.text: Constantine moved the capital to Constantinople, and Christianity became the leading religion.

steps.title: The West falls
steps.text: The western empire broke apart under pressure from Germanic peoples; the last western emperor was deposed in 476.

steps.title: The East lives on
steps.text: The eastern half, the Byzantine Empire, lasted another thousand years until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

title: China’s dynastic cycle
summary: Rise, peak, decline and replacement, from the Shang to the Republic.

steps.title: Shang bronze and oracle bones
steps.text: The Shang left the first Chinese writing and great bronze vessels.

steps.title: The Mandate of Heaven
steps.text: The Zhou overthrew the Shang and claimed Heaven had given them the right to rule, an idea used by later dynasties.

steps.title: The first emperor
steps.text: Qin unified China, standardising writing, money and measures, but collapsed only 15 years later.

steps.title: The Han
steps.text: The Han built a lasting model: Confucian officials, the Silk Road and paper.

steps.title: Division
steps.text: When the Han collapsed, China split into three kingdoms and then centuries of division.

steps.title: Reunification
steps.text: The Sui reunited China and built the Grand Canal, but fell after costly wars.

steps.title: Tang golden age
steps.text: The Tang presided over a golden age of poetry, trade and power, until the An Lushan Rebellion.

steps.title: Song inventions
steps.text: The Song era brought paper money, printing, the compass and gunpowder weapons.

steps.title: Mongol rule
steps.text: Kublai Khan’s Yuan dynasty ruled all of China, the first time foreign conquerors did so.

steps.title: The Ming
steps.text: The Ming restored Chinese rule, sent Zheng He’s fleets abroad and built the Forbidden City.

steps.title: The Qing
steps.text: The Manchu Qing built China’s largest empire, but in the 19th century faced rebellion and foreign pressure.

steps.title: The end of the dynasties
steps.text: Revolution ended 2,000 years of emperors in 1912 and created the Republic of China.

title: Kingdoms of Southeast Asia
summary: Sea empires, temple cities and trading ports, 680–1963.

steps.title: Srivijaya rules the straits
steps.text: From Sumatra, Srivijaya controlled the sea lanes between India and China and became a centre of Buddhist learning.

steps.title: Borobudur
steps.text: In Java, the Sailendra kings built Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument in the world.

steps.title: Temples of Bagan
steps.text: In Myanmar, the Pagan kings built thousands of Buddhist temples on the plain of Bagan.

steps.title: Angkor
steps.text: The Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat and a huge city fed by reservoirs and canals.

steps.title: Majapahit
steps.text: From East Java, Majapahit claimed influence over much of today’s Indonesia, guided by Gajah Mada.

steps.title: Melaka
steps.text: Melaka became the great port where traders from China, India and Arabia met, and spread Islam in the region.

steps.title: The Portuguese arrive
steps.text: The Portuguese captured Melaka in 1511; its royal line moved on to found Johor.

steps.title: Dutch and British
steps.text: European companies and empires divided the region, drawing borders that still shape Malaysia and Indonesia.

steps.title: Independence
steps.text: After the Second World War the region became independent; Malaysia was formed in 1963.

title: The Age of Exploration
summary: Ocean voyages that joined the world together, and the human cost, 1405–1815.

steps.title: Zheng He’s fleets
steps.text: Decades before Europeans, Ming China sent huge fleets across the Indian Ocean as far as East Africa.

steps.title: Columbus crosses the Atlantic
steps.text: Sailing for Spain, Columbus reached the Caribbean, beginning lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.

steps.title: Round Africa to India
steps.text: Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to India, opening a sea route for the spice trade.

steps.title: Conquest in the Americas
steps.text: Spanish conquerors, helped by local allies and epidemics, toppled the Aztec and then the Inca empires.

steps.title: Across the Pacific
steps.text: Manila galleons linked Asia and the Americas, swapping American silver for Chinese silk.

steps.title: Companies and empires
steps.text: The Dutch East India Company, one of the first joint-stock companies, built a trading empire in Asia.

steps.title: The Atlantic slave trade
steps.text: About 12.5 million Africans were forcibly shipped to the Americas to work on plantations.

title: The Mongol storm
summary: How steppe horsemen built the largest land empire in history, 1206–1480.

steps.title: Genghis Khan unites the steppe
steps.text: Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and took the title Genghis Khan in 1206.

steps.title: The empire expands
steps.text: Mongol horse archers conquered northern China and Central Asia, destroying cities that resisted.

steps.title: Rus’ falls
steps.text: Batu’s armies sacked Kiev; the Golden Horde would rule the Rus’ principalities for two centuries.

steps.title: Baghdad is sacked
steps.text: Hulegu sacked Baghdad, ending the Abbasid Caliphate, and founded the Ilkhanate in Iran.

steps.title: The Mamluks stop them
steps.text: At Ain Jalut the Mamluks of Egypt defeated a Mongol army, halting expansion into Africa.

steps.title: Kublai rules China
steps.text: Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty and ruled all of China from Khanbaliq (Beijing).

steps.title: Trade and plague
steps.text: The Mongol peace boosted Silk Road trade, but also helped plague spread across Eurasia.

steps.title: The khanates break up
steps.text: By 1480 the khanates had split or fallen; Muscovy stopped paying tribute to the Great Horde.

title: The rise of Islam and its golden age
summary: From Mecca to Baghdad and Córdoba: faith, empire and learning, 622–1258.

steps.title: The Hijra
steps.text: Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina in 622, year one of the Islamic calendar.

steps.title: Rapid conquests
steps.text: Under the first caliphs, Arab armies defeated Byzantium and Persia in a few decades.

steps.title: The Umayyads
steps.text: The Umayyad Caliphate ruled from Damascus, from Spain to Central Asia.

steps.title: Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
steps.text: The Abbasids built Baghdad; scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works and advanced algebra and astronomy.

steps.title: Cairo and al-Azhar
steps.text: The Fatimids founded Cairo and the al-Azhar mosque, one of the oldest universities.

steps.title: Ibn Sina and al-Biruni
steps.text: Scholars such as Ibn Sina (medicine) and al-Biruni (science) wrote works used for centuries.

steps.title: Philosophy in Spain
steps.text: In al-Andalus, Ibn Rushd’s commentaries on Aristotle later shaped European universities.

steps.title: The fall of Baghdad
steps.text: The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 is often taken as the end of the golden age.

title: Great kingdoms of Africa
summary: Gold, trade and empire across Africa, from Kush to the Zulu.

steps.title: Kush rules Egypt
steps.text: Kings from Kush, south of Egypt, conquered Egypt and ruled as its 25th Dynasty.

steps.title: Aksum
steps.text: Aksum, in Ethiopia and Eritrea, minted coins, raised giant stelae and adopted Christianity.

steps.title: Ghana, land of gold
steps.text: Ghana grew rich by taxing gold and salt carried across the Sahara by camel caravans.

steps.title: Great Zimbabwe
steps.text: In southern Africa, Great Zimbabwe built huge dry-stone walls and traded gold to the coast.

steps.title: Mansa Musa
steps.text: Mali’s ruler made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with so much gold that it changed prices in Cairo.

steps.title: Kilwa and the Swahili Coast
steps.text: Swahili ports like Kilwa linked Africa to Arabia, India and China.

steps.title: Songhai and Timbuktu
steps.text: Songhai controlled the Niger trade, and Timbuktu was a centre of Islamic scholarship.

steps.title: Asante and the Golden Stool
steps.text: The Asante united under the Golden Stool and grew rich on gold and trade.

steps.title: Resistance and conquest
steps.text: The Zulu defeated a British army at Isandlwana, but by 1900 European powers had conquered most of Africa.

steps.title: Adwa
steps.text: Ethiopia defeated an Italian invasion at Adwa and stayed independent.

title: Empires and independence
summary: How European empires spread across the world, and how colonies won freedom, 1757–1965.

steps.title: The East India Company
steps.text: Victory at Plassey let the British East India Company take control of Bengal.

steps.title: Opium and treaties
steps.text: Britain fought China to protect the opium trade, forcing open Chinese ports.

steps.title: Rebellion in India
steps.text: A great uprising in India led Britain to rule India directly from 1858.

steps.title: The Scramble for Africa
steps.text: At the Berlin Conference, European powers set rules for dividing Africa among themselves.

steps.title: Indian independence
steps.text: After decades of mass protest, India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, with a violent partition.

steps.title: Indonesia and Malaya
steps.text: Indonesia declared independence in 1945; Malaya became independent in 1957.

steps.title: The Year of Africa
steps.text: In 1960 seventeen African countries became independent.

steps.title: Algeria
steps.text: After a long war, Algeria won independence from France in 1962.

title: The world wars
summary: Two global wars and the world they made, 1914–1945.

steps.title: A shot in Sarajevo
steps.text: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand set off the First World War.

steps.title: The First World War
steps.text: Trench warfare, machine guns and gas killed millions.

steps.title: Revolution in Russia
steps.text: War and hardship brought revolution; the Bolsheviks took power.

steps.title: The peace
steps.text: The Treaty of Versailles redrew the map and punished Germany.

steps.title: The Great Depression
steps.text: A global economic collapse helped extremist movements rise.

steps.title: The Second World War
steps.text: Germany, Italy and Japan fought the Allies; the war became the deadliest in history.

steps.title: The Holocaust
steps.text: Nazi Germany murdered around six million Jews and many others.

steps.title: Turning point
steps.text: The Soviet victory at Stalingrad turned the war in Europe.

steps.title: The atomic age
steps.text: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki preceded Japan’s surrender.
